text: {"headline":"Elevated 99215 billing persists at every complexity level, including routine acute visits on patients with no chronic conditions, but the single documented 99215 is too thin to confirm or refute upcoding.","leaning":"pattern_consistent_with_upcoding","interpretation":"The claims pattern does not look like a sicker panel. The excess 99215 share appears in every complexity stratum, not just among multimorbid patients, and about half of the 99215s fall on patients with 0–1 conditions. The sampled low-complexity 99215s are mostly routine problems: upper respiratory infections (C0199451, C0199894), UTIs (C0199334, C0199875), low back pain (C0199115-type M54.50 claims such as C0199700) and follow-up visits (C0199556, C0199579). Complex-patient 99215s such as C0200093 and C0199962 are plausible, but they do not explain the excess. The documentation cannot settle the question: records came back for only a small fraction of claims and cover just one 99215. That claim, C0199784, is an 18-year-old with an upper respiratory infection documented as high MDM with no time recorded, which is itself worth scrutiny as a possibly inflated or templated note rather than reassurance. A reviewer should first request charts for the sampled low-complexity 99215 claims listed above and check whether the MDM elements, time and any tests ordered genuinely support high complexity for these routine diagnoses."}
